summary:
Baden-Württemberg stands under Germany's national framework. Federal constitutional and equality protections apply nationwide, identity documents, marriage law and legal gender recognition are uniform across the Länder, and no Land can remove that floor.

Custody placement is the sharpest documented exposure for a trans visitor. German prisons operate under statutory separation with a binary men and women housing model, and the Criminological Research Institute of Lower Saxony (KFN) reports that placement corresponding to a prisoner's gender identity has been practised only in exceptional cases; it runs a research project on the situation of transgender people in prison. The exception is applied inconsistently. In July 2026 a convicted far-right extremist holding a legally recognised female gender entry was transferred from a women's prison to a men's prison after public outcry, authorities citing the safety of prisoners at the women's facility. In the earlier Penelope Frank case, reported by DW in August 2023, a climate activist with a legal male registration faced assignment to a men's prison on conviction, and the reporting described German prisons as offering few safe spaces for trans inmates.

Baden-Württemberg carries the older rule. A constitutional-law analysis published on 18 March 2026 found that placement rules in most Länder have stood unchanged since the 1970s and are now being revised: a new Art. 17 of Rhineland-Palatinate's prison act has been in force since 1 March 2026, and Bavarian, Saxon and Hamburg rules have also recently entered into force, giving a majority of Länder revised provisions. Only Bremen's law explicitly references the registered gender entry, with other Länder doing so implicitly. Baden-Württemberg is not named in the analysis, and its own prison law retains the unrevised 1970s-era placement rules, so a trans visitor taken into custody here stands under the pre-revision regime.

Legal gender recognition on paper is straightforward. The Self-Determination Act, passed in April 2024 by 374 votes to 251, took effect on 1 November 2024 and allows transgender, intersex and non-binary adults to change their legal gender by self-determination with three months' notice, replacing the Transsexuals Act of 1980 whose surgery and sterilisation requirements the Federal Constitutional Court struck down in January 2011. A 'divers' marker has been available on birth certificates, passports and driving licences since 1 January 2019 under the Third Gender Act, but it requires a doctor's statement confirming intersex status and was clarified in April 2019 as applying to intersex people only, not transgender people.

Airport screening has produced a specific documented complaint. The DJ and producer BASHKKA filed a legal complaint under the General Act on Equal Treatment over a screening at Frankfurt Airport on 23 November 2024, stating that officers deliberately disregarded her gender identity in what she called a targeted, degrading act of transphobic harassment; she provided Resident Advisor, reporting in June 2025, a copy of her statement to the airport.

Access to women-protected spaces is contested in the leisure sector. A Deutscher Sauna-Bund guideline issued in January 2025 restricting women's saunas to persons whose primary sex characteristics correspond set off public argument over registered trans women's access after the Self-Determination Act took effect, amid fears that the self-declaration route would be misused.

Discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity is prohibited in health services and in education under the General Act on Equal Treatment, in force since 18 August 2006. A nationwide ban on conversion therapy for minors has been in place since May 2020, carrying penalties of up to one year in prison for practitioners and fines of €30,000 for offering, promoting or referring minors to such treatment.

Asylum and admission policy moved against LGBTI protection during 2025. In June the Federal Cabinet proposed designating Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia as safe countries of origin despite LGBTI people facing imprisonment there, and in August the governing coalition announced it would end humanitarian admission programmes, including the Afghanistan scheme for persecuted LGBTI people.

A victim-support infrastructure exists. The German STOP the HATE campaign runs a counselling finder sorted by topic, emergency guidance including an LSBTIQ* crisis line, and a hate-crime knowledge base covering underreporting, evidence preservation, witness support and reporting channels.
tangentialFactors:
The pace of prison-law revision varies sharply between Länder, and the direction is toward accommodation. Alongside Rhineland-Palatinate's Art. 17, in force since 1 March 2026 with no press coverage at all, Bavarian, Saxon and Hamburg rules have recently entered into force. The Verfassungsblog analysis argues that no constitutional duty exists to anchor placement to the registered gender entry, since a prisoner self-declaration would intrude less on the right to gender self-determination, a position that leaves the constitutional floor contested rather than settled.

Cases elsewhere in Germany show outcomes going both ways. DW reported on 16 July 2026 that Marla-Svenja Liebich, whose gender entry had been changed to female at the end of 2024 under the Self-Determination Act, was transferred to a men's prison after her extradition from Czechia despite being legally registered as a woman; the chief prosecutor for Halle had stated in August 2025 that she would serve an 18-month sentence for incitement at Chemnitz women's prison with placement reviewed at intake. Critics of the transfer characterised the gender change as an abuse of the self-determination law.

Institutional practice in other Länder is more developed than in Baden-Württemberg. The Berlin prison service maintains an official information page for trans people in custody setting out rules and contacts across the city's facilities, and reporting from Berlin on how saunas and similar venues handle trans women followed months of argument over women-protected spaces. The Federal Anti-Discrimination Office found that a July 2025 ban on gender-inclusive language imposed by the Education Minister in her own ministry contradicted constitutional equality protection, evidence of official hostility at federal level. The KFN's continuing research project on transgender prisoners is the main structured monitoring of how the exceptional-case rule operates.
localsOnly:
Residents changing legal gender do so under the Self-Determination Act with three months' notice, without surgery or sterilisation; the procedure and the resulting documents are the same in Baden-Württemberg as in every other Land. The 'divers' marker remains available only on a doctor's statement confirming intersex status.

Residents have standing under the General Act on Equal Treatment in health services and education, and can use the German STOP the HATE campaign's counselling finder, its LSBTIQ* crisis line and its hate-crime knowledge base, which sets out evidence preservation, witness support and reporting channels. Practitioners offering, promoting or referring minors to conversion therapy face up to one year in prison and fines of €30,000.

Residents held in Baden-Württemberg's prisons are placed under the Land's unrevised 1970s-era rules rather than the newer provisions in force in Rhineland-Palatinate, Bavaria, Saxony and Hamburg, and the KFN's research project is the documented route for scrutiny of how those rules are applied.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Baden-Württemberg-specific source in this inventory reports an intake decision, a placement outcome or a state-level directive; the Land's position is established by the absence of its name from the 18 March 2026 analysis and by its retention of unrevised placement rules. Whether any revision is under way in Baden-Württemberg's justice ministry is unresolved on these sources.

The Verfassungsblog analysis states that placement rules in most Länder have stood unchanged since the 1970s, but it does not give the text of Baden-Württemberg's provision, so the exact statutory wording applicable here is not sourced.

The Frankfurt Airport screening account rests on the complainant's own statement as reported by Resident Advisor; the outcome of her complaint under the General Act on Equal Treatment is not in the inventory. Whether comparable complaints have been filed at airports in Baden-Württemberg, and how the Land's prison administration treats the registered gender entry at intake, are not sourced.
